name: Amira Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing law, first year. I live with my mum in Harlow Green and take the 7:10 bus, which is fifty minutes each way. Lectures are Monday to Thursday, and I work at Dunmore's Bakery on Saturdays and Sundays, six hours a day, on the counter. The rest of my time is reading cases in the library, which is slower than I expected.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has surprised you most about the first weeks?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: How many people on my course just paste questions into a chatbot. I don't, and I don't plan to. I'd rather struggle through a case myself and understand it. Also, nobody warned me the loan arrives late, so in October I was counting coins for bus fares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a lot of noise about nothing. The bakery has a new till that prints orders, and that's about it. I'd tell my friends not to panic over every headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it still worries me, because the AI barely matters when the real problem is money. My loan covers fees but not my bus pass, and I have under a month saved. If the bakery cuts one shift, I'm in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Keep both weekend shifts, keep reading cases by hand and put twenty pounds a week into a jar for the bus. I'd also ask my manager Pauline if I can get more hours in December.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, mostly. Not scared, just tired in advance. A quiet world is fine, but a quiet world with my wage staying the same while prices creep up isn't comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be uneasy even if little changes. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bus fares went up again this year and my wage didn't. That's what I mean. Nothing dramatic needs to happen for me to be squeezed. I'm already in that spot, with no cushion at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be responsible if bosses use it to cut hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies and the council that cut routes, not the technology. Bakery owners and big firms decide who works. I'd want a union to make sure part-timers like me get fair hours, and a bus pass for students.

say: I'd tell friends the **hype** is overblown and people shouldn't panic.
I'd say what matters is wages and bus fares, not robots.
think: My real worry is **money**: under a month saved and a thin loan.
One cut shift at the bakery would hurt me straight away.
do: Keep both weekend **shifts** at Dunmore's Bakery.
Put twenty pounds a week into a jar for the bus pass.
Ask Pauline for extra **hours** in December.
feel: Tired in advance, not scared, because the **squeeze** is already here.
S0.quote: Nothing dramatic needs to happen for me to be squeezed. I'm already in that spot, with no cushion at all.
fieldNote: Her worry is about **money** and part-time hours, not AI itself.
Blames employers and the council, which fits her union-friendly outlook.
Never uses AI tools, so this scenario barely touches her routine.

steps.text: Keep both weekend shifts at Dunmore's Bakery
Save twenty pounds a week in a jar for bus fares
Ask the union and the student office about a bus pass subsidy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the firms using it to save money, not to help anyone. Paralegals and clerks are the ones who'd lose out. I'd say it publicly because somebody should say it, even if I'm only eighteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the entry jobs I want, like trainee paralegal, are the first ones software takes. Document checking is exactly what it does well. I'm scared I'll finish three years of debt and find the door half shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on my course and refuse to hide from it. Maybe I'd go to one workshop on how firms use it, so I at least know what I'm up against. I'd join the student union's campaign on graduate jobs and keep the bakery shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some anger mixed in. It feels unfair to carry the debt while the firms save the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Law has a lot of reading and checking. How soon would that reach the jobs you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From what I read, law firms already use software to review contracts. If a trainee spends two years checking documents, and software does it in a minute, the training post disappears. I don't see how new ones appear fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone on your course who uses AI for essays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that doing it yourself builds a skill nobody can take off you. But I'd also admit I might be wrong, and they might be the smart ones. That's the part that scares me.

say: I'd say firms use AI to **save money**, not to help workers.
I'd back the student union on **graduate jobs** out loud.
think: Trainee **paralegal** work is exactly what software takes first.
I fear three years of **debt** and a half-shut door.
do: Join the student union's campaign on graduate **jobs**.
Go to one **workshop** on how law firms use AI.
Keep the bakery shifts and keep reading cases by hand.
feel: **Anxious** and angry that the debt falls on students while firms save.
S1.quote: If a trainee spends two years checking documents, and software does it in a minute, the training post disappears.
fieldNote: Strong **anger** at firms rather than at the technology.
Sees her own course as exposed, which is accurate for law.
Honest enough to admit classmates who use AI might be the smart ones.

steps.text: Join the student union campaign on graduate jobs
Attend one workshop on how law firms use AI
Keep the Saturday and Sunday bakery shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why governments need to act now. Two years is nothing. I'd write to my MP, join marches and demand support for people who lose jobs, whatever the technology does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my degree would be worth very little. By the time I graduate in 2029, thinking work is already done by machines. I'd have the debt and a certificate for a job that doesn't exist. I don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd stop adding to the loan and think hard about leaving. Maybe I'd look for work in something hands-on for the three years before robots come, like care work or baking. I'd also ask Mum whether we can stay put and pool money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I was running up a down escalator. Everything I planned for is gone and I'm eighteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the degree itself in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dropping out feels like failing, and my mum scraped to get me here. But carrying on to owe thousands for a useless degree is worse. I'd probably talk to the university's money advice team first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you lean on if it gets that bad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, and the union, and honestly the government. If nobody has time to prepare, then somebody has to catch us. I'd want a guaranteed income, even a small one, so a year of dropping out doesn't ruin me.

say: I'd write to my **MP** and demand support for people who lose work.
I'd say two years is **no time** for anyone to prepare.
think: My law degree could be worth **nothing** by 2029, with the debt still there.
Dropping out feels like **failing** my mum, who scraped to get me here.
do: See the university **money advice** team about stopping the loan.
Look for hands-on work like care or baking for three years.
Write to my MP and join a **march**.
feel: **Alarmed**, like running up a down escalator at eighteen.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I was running up a down escalator. Everything I planned for is gone and I'm eighteen.
fieldNote: Her fear is about the **debt** outliving the degree's value.
Guilt towards her mother shapes the dropout decision.
Turns to **politics** and the state, consistent with her progressive outlook.

steps.text: Write to my MP asking for income support for displaced workers
Look into care or bakery work as a hands-on fallback
See the university money advice team about pausing the loan
Stop spending on anything except bus fares and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a little breathing room, but it's still too fast for governments to get organised. I'd push for retraining funds and a shorter working week, and I'd say it loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd finish the degree, but with a plan B. By 2031 I'm twenty-three with a new law degree, in the middle of the change. That's right at the worst point to be looking for a first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my course for the first two years, and put every spare hour into skills the machines are slower at, like speaking up in court or dealing with clients. I'd also pay back a bit of the loan whenever I can, even five pounds, and talk to the careers office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. Five years feels like enough time to do something, which is better than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you stay in the law degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be dropping out. With five, I can finish the first degree and see if courtroom work stays human. Standing in a courtroom is hands-on in a way. Robots are three years behind, so that part of law gives me a little hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between the two-year and five-year versions for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have more say over my own money and my own life. I'd feel less like a cog being thrown off a belt.

say: I'd push for **retraining funds** and a shorter working week.
I'd say five years is a little room but still too fast.
think: I'd finish the degree but with a **plan B**.
Graduating in 2031 means hunting a first job at the **worst** moment.
do: Stay on the course for **two years** and then review.
Practise speaking and client skills at the debating society.
Repay five pounds of the **loan** whenever I can.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, because five years is enough to act.
S3.quote: Five years feels like enough time to do something, which is better than panic.
fieldNote: Time to act **changes** her from dropout to cautious finisher.
Finds hope in courtroom work being hands-on.
Still thinks the timing of her first job hunt is the real danger.

steps.text: Stay on the law degree for two years then review
Join the debating society to practise speaking and client skills
Repay five pounds of the loan whenever the wage allows
Push the student union for retraining funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds almost normal. I'd say to my friends that we have time to build good rules and good unions. I'd be quite hopeful in public and keep up the pressure on politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think the world will look very different by the time I'm twenty-eight. But a decade lets me build a career and some savings. The wage jobs I know will change, but I can change with them slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work through the degree properly, then try to get into a firm early and learn how they use AI. I'd also finally try one of these tools in my second or third year, so I'm not blind. And I'd save even a small amount each month so I'm not on zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not anxious. There's time, but I'm already carrying money worries that this picture doesn't fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be about 28 by then. What would your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By twenty-eight I'd like to be qualified and working, maybe renting a flat of my own near my mum. If the world holds together, that's possible. It depends on pay not collapsing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting out in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to learn the basics by hand first, then use the tools later. And join a union early. A decade is enough to do both if you start now.

say: I'd say we have **time** to build good rules and strong unions.
I'd stay hopeful in public and keep pressing politicians.
think: The world will look very **different** by twenty-eight, but I can adapt slowly.
A decade lets me build a **career** and some savings.
do: Finish the law degree and aim for an early **firm** placement.
Try one AI tool in my **second** year so I'm not blind.
Save a small amount every **month** from the bakery wage.
feel: **Uneasy**, not anxious, because money worries stay even with time.
S4.quote: I'd tell my cousin to learn the basics by hand first, then use the tools later.
fieldNote: Even her resistant attitude to **AI tools** softens when there is a decade.
Plans stay modest and tied to savings and a union.
Mood is set by her thin cushion more than by the technology.

steps.text: Finish the law degree and apply for an early firm placement
Try one AI tool in second year to understand it
Save a small amount from the bakery wage each month
Join the student union and stay active through the degree

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. It leaves no time to move, and I'd have the debt and nothing to show for it. What would help is simple: income support if jobs vanish, student debt paused if the degree stops paying, and unions strong enough to speak for part-timers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe just that people my age aren't lazy about this. We're thinking about it harder than adults assume. I'd like someone senior to ask us what would help before deciding for us.

headlineQuote: People my age aren't lazy about this. We're thinking about it harder than adults assume.
portrait: Amira is an eighteen-year-old **law student** who lives with her mum and works weekends at a bakery.
She has a thin cushion, a late loan and under a month saved, so money shapes every answer.
Progressive and union-minded, she blames firms and councils rather than the technology.
She resists AI tools but admits classmates who use them might be smarter.
Her mood climbs to **alarmed** in the two-year case, where she'd think of dropping out.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because there'd be no time and the debt would remain.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** if jobs vanish, and student debt paused if the degree stops paying.
Strong **unions** that speak for part-time workers like her.
